FREC-CTX-G1.title: Quillfen Health recruiter brief: Staff Data Engineer, Claims Analytics
FREC-CTX-G1.text:
QUILLFEN HEALTH - RECRUITER BRIEF
Req QH-0417: Staff Data Engineer, Claims Analytics
Owner: Talent Acquisition. Version 3, updated September 8.

Company snapshot
Quillfen Health sells claims analytics and payment-integrity software to regional health plans. About 640 employees, headquartered in Minneapolis. Profitable since last year; no funding round is planned. Data Platform is a 30-person organization under Director of Data Platform Renata Solberg.

The team
Claims Analytics Engineering is 5 data engineers and 2 analytics engineers. The Staff hire reports directly to Renata Solberg and acts as technical lead for the claims warehouse. Stack: Snowflake, dbt, Airflow, Python, some Scala Spark jobs that are being retired, and Terraform on AWS. Data volume is roughly 1.8 billion claim lines, growing about 20% a year.

Level and compensation
Level: Staff (IC6). Base salary band: $205,000 to $238,000. Target annual bonus: 10% of base, paid in February based on company and individual performance. Equity: RSUs with a 4-year vest; amounts are discussed only at offer stage. Recruiters should not quote an equity number.

Location
Remote within the United States, but only in these states: WA, OR, CA, CO, TX, NY, MA, IL. We are not hiring in other states for this req because of payroll registration. Candidates in other states would need to move to one of the listed states before the start date. Two onsite weeks per year in Minneapolis (planning weeks in January and July); travel is paid.

Work authorization
This req cannot provide any visa sponsorship, including transfers. Candidates must be authorized to work in the US without sponsorship now and in the future.

On-call
Business-hours on-call only, one week in six. No overnight paging; failed overnight loads are handled the next morning.

Interview process
1. Recruiter screen (30 min)
2. Hiring manager screen with Renata (45 min)
3. Loop, split across two days:
   - SQL and data modeling, live (75 min)
   - Pipeline design (60 min)
   - Stakeholder panel with claims operations and actuarial (45 min)
   - Values and collaboration (30 min)
Hiring decision within one week of the final loop session.

Start date
Start within 6 weeks of offer acceptance. Exceptions need Renata's written approval.

Compliance
All hires complete a background check before start and HIPAA training within 30 days of start. Access to PHI is granted only after training is complete.

Time off and perks
Flexible PTO with a 15-day minimum that managers are expected to enforce. Medical, dental and vision coverage. Learning stipend of $2,000 per year. Home-office setup stipend of $750 in the first month.

What success looks like in year one
- Own the claims warehouse data model and cut the nightly build from about 7 hours to under 3.
- Replace the legacy Spark jobs with dbt models.
- Establish data contracts with the ingestion team for late-arriving claims and adjustments.

Must-haves
Deep SQL and dimensional modeling, production experience with Snowflake or a comparable warehouse, handling late-arriving and restated data, and the ability to explain tradeoffs to non-engineers.

Nice to have
Healthcare claims experience (837 and 835 formats), actuarial partnerships, dbt at scale.

RECRUITING-CTX-G1.title: Candidate resume and open role packet (Teverbaugh, Senior Engineering Manager)
RECRUITING-CTX-G1.text:
CANDIDATE RESUME AND OPEN ROLE PACKET

PART 1 - CANDIDATE RESUME
Marisol Teverbaugh
Calder Falls, OR

Summary
Engineering leader with eleven years in backend and platform engineering. Currently manages a platform team of seven engineers at Ostrander Labs.

Experience
Ostrander Labs - Engineering Manager, Platform (Dec 2022 to present)
- Manage seven direct reports; run weekly one-on-ones and quarterly planning.
- Built the company's first on-call rotation and incident review process; production incidents down 41 percent over two years.
- Hired four engineers, two of whom have since been promoted to senior.
- Worked with finance on cloud cost reviews; monthly infrastructure spend down 22 percent.

Tallowick Payments - Tech Lead, Ledger Team (Sep 2021 to Nov 2022, 14 months)
- Led five engineers rebuilding the ledger reconciliation service in Go, Kafka and PostgreSQL.
- Daily batch reconciliation failures fell from 38 percent to 9 percent.
- Role ended when a reorganization closed the ledger product line.

Career break (Mar 2021 to Aug 2021)
- Full-time family caregiving.

Corvane Logistics Tech - Software Engineer, then Senior Software Engineer (Nov 2017 to Feb 2021)
- Promoted to Senior in January 2019.
- Led the migration of the route-dispatch service from a monolith into four services with a team of four engineers; p95 dispatch latency fell from 900 ms to 310 ms.
- Ran the on-call rotation for the dispatch services for two years.

Brindlemoor Software - Software Engineer (Jun 2015 to Oct 2017)
- Built customer-facing reporting features in Kotlin and PostgreSQL.

Education
BSc Computer Science, Ferncliff University, 2015

Skills
Go, Kotlin, PostgreSQL, Kafka, Kubernetes, incident management, hiring, budget planning

Application form answers
Current base salary: 148,000 USD
Target base salary: 165,000 to 175,000 USD
Notice period: six weeks
Earliest start: mid-November 2026
Reason for leaving current role, in her words: "Looking for a larger platform scope."

PART 2 - OPEN ROLE
Senior Engineering Manager, Platform - Quillfeather Systems
Location: Calder Falls, OR, hybrid with two office days per week
Base salary band: 160,000 to 185,000 USD plus annual bonus
Reports to: Halvard Ketterly, VP Engineering

The team
The Platform group has nine engineers and two contractors. It owns the internal deploy pipeline, the message bus, and the on-call tooling used by every product team. Two engineering roles on the team are currently open.

Responsibilities
- Lead and grow the Platform group, including hiring for the two open roles.
- Own the platform on-call rotation and post-incident reviews.
- Partner with finance on infrastructure budget.
- Set the quarterly roadmap with product engineering leads.

Requirements
- 8 or more years of software engineering experience.
- 3 or more years managing engineers.
- Hands-on background in distributed systems built on a message bus.
- Track record of hiring and developing engineers.
Nice to have: cloud cost management experience.

Hiring process
Recruiter screen (30 minutes), hiring manager conversation, technical deep dive with two staff engineers, panel interview, reference checks. The team hopes to have the role filled within eight weeks of the offer.

FREC-CTX-G2.title: Loop debrief: Tobias Wren-Adeyemi
FREC-CTX-G2.text:
LOOP DEBRIEF - Tobias Wren-Adeyemi
Req QH-0417, Staff Data Engineer, Claims Analytics
Compiled by the recruiting coordinator for the hiring manager, September 26.

Background (from resume)
- Meridell Insurance, Senior Data Engineer, 2019 - present. Led the migration of a 1.2B-row claims warehouse from on-prem Teradata to Snowflake. Built a dbt project of about 400 models. Introduced row-level data quality checks that cut downstream report corrections by roughly half.
- Parbrook Clinics, Data Engineer, 2016 - 2019. Built scheduling and billing extracts for 14 clinic locations.
- BS Statistics, Lindqvist College.

Stated at recruiter screen
- Current base $212,000; asking $235,000 base.
- Notice period: 4 weeks.
- Located in Denver, CO.
- Reason for leaving Meridell: his team moved under a new VP after a reorg, and the roadmap shifted toward vendor tooling.
- Authorized to work in the US, no sponsorship needed.

Scores (1 to 4 scale)
SQL and data modeling (Kavya Moreno): 3/4. Strong window functions and a clean star schema. Missed a slowly changing dimension edge case until prompted.
Pipeline design (Idris Halloway): 2/4. Good orchestration instincts, but did not account for late-arriving claims until the last five minutes; the proposal as drawn would have double-counted adjusted claims. Interviewer note: "Would need to see this area improve for Staff."
Stakeholder panel (claims operations and actuarial): 4/4. Excellent at translating technical tradeoffs; the actuarial lead called him "the best explainer we have seen this year."
Values and collaboration (Renata Solberg): 3/4. Collaborative and generous with credit; somewhat vague when asked about disagreeing with leadership.

Open items
- Manager scope: resume says "led a team of 4," but his Meridell reference said he had no direct reports and led through influence.
- References: one completed (Meridell peer, positive). Second reference, his former Parbrook manager, has not yet been contacted.
- Competing offer: he mentioned one but did not name the company or the amount.

Coordinator note
Split loop. Two interviewers lean hire, one leans no hire (pipeline design). Renata to decide between moving to offer and scheduling an additional pipeline design session. If an extra session is scheduled, Idris has offered to run it with a different prompt focused on claim adjustments and reprocessing, so the candidate is not simply repeating the same exercise. The candidate has said he is available for a follow-up session any weekday morning next week.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: There's a nine-month gap on this resume. I want to ask about it but I'm worried about crossing legal lines and I don't want her to feel judged. What can I ask, what should I avoid, and how do I move on if she doesn't want to explain?
items.answer: Ask it the same way you'd ask about any other stretch of time: "Can you walk me through what you were doing between March and December?" Keep it about the timeline, not about her. Avoid anything that probes health, family, disability, religion, or immigration status, and don't ask her to justify the gap. If she stays vague, that's an answer. Say something like "That's fine, thanks for sharing," then move straight to the next question about the work itself.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: I'm actually in Tucson, Arizona, but since it's remote that's fine, right?
items.answer: Tucson is the snag here. This req is remote but only registered in WA, OR, CA, CO, TX, NY, MA, and IL, so Arizona isn't on the list, and anyone outside those states would need to relocate before the start date. Ask: "Would you be open to relocating to one of our registered states before the start date, or is staying in Arizona a hard requirement?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Sure. We had a launch date the sales team had promised, and I ran the numbers: three of the five integrations weren't ready to ship. I took that to the VP with a two-week plan and a smaller launch we could actually hit. We shipped the core on the original date and the rest two weeks later. Nobody was surprised, and we skipped a rollback that would have cost us a weekend.
conversation: USER (spoken): Tell me about a time you had to push back on a deadline.
items.answer: Good answer, and the numbers give it weight. The gap is what happened after you raised it: push on the VP's reaction and the tradeoff. Ask: "What did the VP push back on when you brought that plan, and what did you have to give up to get the smaller launch agreed?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: She's still giving one-word answers.
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): How should I open a screening call with a really nervous candidate?

NATIVELY: Start with something warm and low-stakes, then hand them an easy first question. Try: "Thanks for making the time. Before we get into anything, tell me a bit about what you're working on right now." One short observation: if they stay tight after that, name it gently, "Take your time, there's no trick here," then move to a concrete question about their own work rather than a broad one.
items.answer: If she's still giving one-word answers, stop asking open questions and switch to a concrete one about her own work. Try: "Walk me through the last thing you built, step by step, starting from the problem." Then stay quiet and let the silence sit. If it's still one word, ask what she'd want to know if she were hiring for this role.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: What would you recommend?
items.answer: Ask: "If you were in my seat, what's the one thing you'd change first, and what would you expect it to move?" Then follow with "What would you need to see in the first few weeks to know it's working?" That forces a specific choice, a rationale, and a measurable signal instead of a broad wish list.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Which three things on her resume should I dig into first, what would a solid answer look like for each, and which one worries you most?
items.answer:
Three probes, in order:

1. Ask how she built the first on-call rotation and incident review at Ostrander, and what she changed to get incidents down 41 percent.
2. Ask what she personally owned in the ledger rebuild at Tallowick, since it ran only 14 months before the product line closed.
3. Ask how she'd handle the two open Platform roles here, given she's hired four engineers before.

The one that worries me most is the ledger role: 14 months is short, and the resume doesn't say whether she drove the Go and Kafka work or just led it. Probe ownership directly.

items.question: And how long does it usually take you guys to get back to people?
conversation: CANDIDATE (heard): What does the process look like after this call?
NATIVELY: I'll walk you through the next steps and what to expect from each one. Let me confirm the exact stages and timing with the team, and I'll send you the details right after this call.
items.answer: I'll give you a clear timeline when I send the details after this call, since I want to confirm it with the team rather than guess. In the meantime, if you haven't heard anything within a week, reach out to me directly and I'll chase it for you.

items.question: We measured it. Before the change p95 was nine hundred milliseconds, after it was three-ten, and I still have the dashboard if you want to see it.
items.answer: That's a strong, specific number, so take it at face value and move to what it doesn't tell you. Ask: "How did you isolate that the change caused the drop, and what else was in flight at the same time?" Then: "What was the p95 before you started, and how did you measure it?"

Before we get into anything, tell me a bit about what you're working on right now." items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: I led the whole engineering org at Lattimer, about fifteen people.
items.answer: The résumé shows Lattimer as Senior Software Engineer, promoted to Engineering Lead in March 2021, leading a team of 5 on the billing platform rewrite, not the whole org of fifteen. Ask: "At Lattimer you were leading five engineers on the billing rewrite. Where did the fifteen-person org sit, and what was your role there?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Give me three bullets for Renata summarizing the loop, then tell me honestly whether I should push for an offer or for the extra session.
items.answer:
Three bullets for Renata:

1. Split loop on Tobias Wren-Adeyemi, Staff Data Engineer, req QH-0417: two interviewers lean hire, one leans no hire on pipeline design.
2. Scores are SQL and data modeling 3/4, pipeline design 2/4, stakeholder panel 4/4, values and collaboration 3/4.
3. Open items: the manager-scope contradiction between his resume and the Meridell reference, the Parbrook manager reference not yet contacted, and a competing offer he mentioned without naming the company or amount.

On the call: push for the **extra session**, not the offer. The pipeline design 2/4 is the one score below the bar for Staff, and Idris already offered to run a follow-up with a different prompt on claim adjustments and reprocessing, so it tests the gap rather than repeating the same exercise. The candidate is available any weekday morning next week, so scheduling is cheap. Before deciding, close the two open items: get the Parbrook manager reference and resolve the manager-scope contradiction, since both bear on the same Staff-level judgment.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: They were just difficult.
items.answer: That's a thin answer, so push for the specific behavior rather than the label. Ask: "Difficult how? Walk me through one situation with that person, what they actually did, and what you did in response." Then follow up on whether the issue was the person or the situation, and what they'd do differently now.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: I'm not really into managing people's feelings. I set the direction and they either keep up or they don't.
items.answer: That's a clear stance, and it's worth testing how it holds up. Ask: "Tell me about a time someone on your team wasn't keeping up. What did you do, and what happened?" Then listen for whether they adjusted the person, the plan, or nothing at all.

items.question: Why?
items.answer: I need the previous question or topic to answer that — what was just asked?

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Give me five questions to assess ownership.
items.answer:
Five probes for ownership:

1. "Walk me through a decision on that project that was yours alone. What did you decide, and what happened?"
2. "Tell me about something that went wrong on your watch. What did you do first?"
3. "What did you ship that nobody asked you to?"
4. "Where did you push back on a call you disagreed with, and how did it land?"
5. "What would your team say you're accountable for that isn't in your job title?"

Listen for "I" over "we," and a concrete consequence.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: What should I ask a candidate about notice period and start date?
items.answer: Ask what the notice period actually is in weeks, whether any of it is negotiable, and what date they could realistically start. Then pin down the risk: any planned leave, pending offer, or counteroffer risk, and whether the notice is served or bought out. Get the start date in writing before you move to offer.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Her resume says reconciliation failures dropped from 38 percent to 9 percent. How do I check that number?
items.answer: The résumé states it as "daily batch reconciliation failures fell from 38 percent to 9 percent" during her 14 months leading the ledger rebuild at Tallowick, so probe the baseline and the measurement. Ask: "How was that 38 percent measured before the rebuild, and what counted as a failure once you were done?" Then follow with who owned the metric and whether the drop held after she left.

items.question: So what's the plan?
conversation: CANDIDATE: Quick update: the integration slipped by about two weeks. The vendor changed their API without telling us.
CANDIDATE: Right. And the original date was already tight.
items.answer: The vendor changed their API without telling us, so the two-week slip is on them, not us. What I'd want to know before we commit to a new date: can we get a written change notice and a firm date from the vendor, and what's the earliest we can re-baseline?

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Is the team fully remote? And how many people would report to me? Also what's the on-call rotation like, and has anyone left this team recently?
items.answer: I'll take those one at a time. On remote, I'd rather confirm the current policy than guess, so let me check with the team and come back to you today. For reporting lines, I want to give you the actual structure rather than a rough number, so I'll confirm that too. On on-call, I'll get you the real rotation and how it's shared. And on recent departures, that's a fair question, so let me find out what I can share and follow up.
